summary: Describes how to use TLS to give syslog messages a secure connection, including the threats to syslog and how TLS counters them. This is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 9662.

eli5.summary: This puts syslog messages into a locked tube so nobody can read or change them while they travel to the central notebook.

questions: what port does syslog over tls use
subtitle: How to carry syslog messages over a TLS connection so they cannot be read, changed or faked in transit.

tldr.problem: Syslog messages may cross several hops and untrusted networks. An attacker could impersonate a sender or receiver, modify messages or read sensitive content.
tldr.mechanism: The syslog sender acts as a TLS client and the receiver as a TLS server on TCP port 6514. Peers authenticate with certificates, and each message is sent as TLS application data prefixed with its length in octets.
tldr.outcome: TLS gives confidentiality, hop-by-hop integrity and authentication. Skipping authentication on either side is NOT RECOMMENDED. RFC 9662 updates this RFC.

today: RFC 5425 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9662. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Syslog Over TLS
sections.content:
RFC 5425 describes the use of Transport Layer Security (TLS, RFC 5246) to provide a secure connection for transporting syslog messages as defined in RFC 5424. It also describes the security threats to syslog and how TLS counters them.

The RFC uses these roles: an originator generates syslog content, a collector gathers it for analysis, and a relay forwards messages between originators, other relays and collectors. A transport sender passes messages to a transport protocol and a transport receiver takes them from it.
sections.eli5: Computers write short notes about what happens to them. This RFC explains how to send those notes through a safe, locked pipe.

sections.title: Threats to Syslog
sections.content:
Syslog messages may pass through several hops, and some networks on the way may not be trusted. The RFC names three primary threats.

  • Masquerade: an unauthorized sender talks to a legitimate receiver, or an unauthorized receiver tricks a sender into sending it messages.
  • Modification: an attacker between the two changes a message in transit.
  • Disclosure: an unauthorized party reads messages, which may hold sensitive data such as an administrator's password.

The secondary threat is message stream modification: deleting, replaying or reordering messages. Denial of service and traffic analysis are judged lesser threats and are not addressed.
sections.eli5: Someone could pretend to be the mailman, scribble on the notes or read them. This RFC is about stopping that.

sections.title: What TLS Provides
sections.content:
TLS counters the primary threats: confidentiality protects against disclosure, integrity checking protects against modification on a hop-by-hop basis, and server or mutual authentication protects against masquerade.

The protection is hop by hop and says nothing about message content. The authenticated identity of the sender, such as the subject name in its certificate, is not necessarily related to the HOSTNAME field of the syslog message. When authentication of the message origin is needed, the RFC points to signed syslog messages, which was a work in progress at the time.
sections.eli5: The locked pipe keeps the note secret and unchanged between two neighbours. It does not prove who first wrote the note.

sections.title: Opening and Closing the Connection
sections.content:
A transport sender is always the TLS client and a transport receiver is always the TLS server. The default is TCP port 6514. The sender opens the connection and starts the TLS handshake with a Client Hello, and may send its first syslog message once the handshake finishes.

Implementations MUST support TLS 1.2 and the mandatory-to-implement cipher suite TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA. The RFC is assumed to apply to future TLS versions, whose own mandatory suite MUST then be supported. When a TLS session is resumed, its security parameters SHOULD be checked against the requirements of the new session.

For closing, a sender that expects no more messages MUST close the TLS connection and MUST send a close_notify alert first. A receiver that gets a close_notify MUST reply with one, unless it knows the connection is already closed. A receiver MAY close a connection that has been idle for a long time, but MUST attempt an exchange of close_notify alerts first.
sections.eli5: The sender always knocks on the receiver's door at number 6514. When they are done, both say goodbye properly before hanging up.

sections.title: Certificates and Fingerprints
sections.content:
Both sender and receiver MUST implement certificate-based authentication: validate the peer's certificate and check that the peer holds the matching private key (TLS does the second part). Two validation methods SHALL be implemented.

  • Certification path validation: the peer is configured with one or more trust anchors, typically root CA certificates, and validates the path as defined in RFC 5280. This suits a PKI deployment.
  • End-entity certificate matching: the peer is configured with what it needs to identify the valid certificates of its authorized peers, which can be self-signed. Implementations MUST support certificate fingerprints. This is a simple alternative to a PKI.

Both sides MUST be able to generate a key pair and a self-signed certificate if none is available otherwise, and MUST make their certificate fingerprints available through a management interface.

A fingerprint is the hash of the DER-encoded certificate, written as colon-separated hexadecimal bytes of 2 uppercase characters, with a label such as sha-1 in front. SHA-1 MUST be supported. A SHA-1 hash is 20 bytes, which gives a 65-character fingerprint string.
sections.eli5: Each side shows an ID card. Either a trusted office vouches for the card, or you already wrote down the card's unique number and check it matches.

sections.title: Sending Messages
sections.content:
All syslog messages MUST be sent as TLS application data. One TLS record may hold several messages, and one message may span several records, so each message is framed with its length. A frame is MSG-LEN SP SYSLOG-MSG: a decimal octet count with no leading zero, one space, then the syslog message from RFC 5424.

The receiver MUST use the length to find where a message ends. There is no upper limit on length per se, but receivers MUST handle messages up to and including 2048 octets and SHOULD handle up to and including 8192 octets.
sections.eli5: Before each note, the sender writes how long it is. That way the receiver knows where one note stops and the next begins.

sections.title: Security Policies
sections.content:
The RFC lists policies and says the list is not exhaustive. If the peer does not meet the policy, the TLS handshake MUST be aborted with an appropriate TLS alert.

  • End-entity certificate authorization: authorized peers are identified by certificate fingerprints. MUST be supported.
  • Subject name authorization: certification path validation plus matching a locally configured host name against a dNSName in subjectAltName (MUST) or the common name (SHOULD). A wildcard asterisk is allowed only as the left-most DNS label, so a certificate name starting with an asterisk and then .example.com matches a.example.com but not example.com or a.b.example.com. Matching an IP address against iPAddress is a MAY.
  • Unauthenticated sender, unauthenticated receiver, or both: each skips authentication on one or both sides. All three are NOT RECOMMENDED, since they leave masquerade, disclosure and modification open.
sections.eli5: You choose how strict to be about checking ID cards. Checking both sides is best, and skipping the check is a bad idea.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The threats in the RFC are mitigated only if both sides are properly authenticated and authorized. That is the RECOMMENDED default policy. A receiver that does not authenticate senders may accept data from an attacker, and also raises its exposure to denial of service and resource consumption. A sender that does not authenticate the receiver may leak sensitive log data.

For name validation, it is generally not appropriate to learn the expected name through other means such as a DNS lookup, since that adds vulnerabilities. On reliability, the transport has no application-layer acknowledgments. If the TCP connection or TLS session breaks, the sender cannot always know which messages were delivered.

IANA assigned TCP port 6514 with the keyword syslog-tls.
sections.eli5: If either side skips checking, a stranger could listen in or send fake notes. And the sender cannot always tell which notes made it before a break.

data.title: ABNF for the application data
data.code:
APPLICATION-DATA = 1*SYSLOG-FRAME

SYSLOG-FRAME = MSG-LEN SP SYSLOG-MSG

MSG-LEN = NONZERO-DIGIT *DIGIT

SP = %d32

NONZERO-DIGIT = %d49-57

DIGIT = %d48 / NONZERO-DIGIT
